raw_text:
Cardiac amyloidosis is an infiltrative cardiomyopathy caused by extracellular myocardial deposition of misfolded proteins arranged as amyloid fibrils. Although many amyloid proteins can involve the heart, most clinically important disease is due to immunoglobulin light-chain amyloidosis (AL) or transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTR), the latter occurring as variant/hereditary ATTR or wild-type ATTR [1,2]. These entities share a restrictive physiology but differ profoundly in tempo, prognosis, and treatment; therefore, accurate typing is the pivotal step after suspicion is raised. Comparative cohorts have shown that AL cardiac amyloidosis often progresses rapidly and carries early mortality, whereas ATTR, particularly wild-type disease, may have a more indolent course despite advanced heart failure at diagnosis [3].

The epidemiology of cardiac amyloidosis has been reshaped by improved recognition. The transthyretin Val122Ile variant is an important cause of late-onset cardiomyopathy among individuals of African ancestry [4]. Autopsy and clinical studies suggest that wild-type transthyretin deposition is common in advanced age [5] and may underlie a proportion of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) [6,7]. ATTR is also increasingly recognized in elderly patients with severe aortic stenosis referred for transcatheter valve replacement [8]. Wild-type ATTR typically affects older men and is frequently preceded by “red flags” such as bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, lumbar spinal stenosis, biceps tendon rupture, atrial arrhythmias, low-flow aortic stenosis, and unexplained concentric left ventricular thickening [9,10].

Clinical presentation ranges from asymptomatic biomarker elevation to advanced restrictive heart failure. Dyspnea, edema, fatigue, orthostatic hypotension, syncope, atrial fibrillation, conduction disease, and intolerance of beta-blockers or renin–angiotensin inhibitors are common. Electrocardiography may show low voltage, pseudo-infarct patterns, or conduction delay, although voltage may be preserved in ATTR. Echocardiography typically demonstrates increased wall thickness, biatrial enlargement, diastolic dysfunction, valve thickening, pericardial effusion, and reduced longitudinal function; relative apical sparing of strain is a useful clue rather than a standalone diagnostic test [11]. Cardiac magnetic resonance adds tissue characterization: diffuse subendocardial or transmural late gadolinium enhancement, abnormal gadolinium kinetics, elevated native T1, and expanded extracellular volume support diagnosis and correlate with disease burden and outcome [12-14].

Bone-avid tracer scintigraphy has transformed noninvasive diagnosis of ATTR cardiac amyloidosis. Strong myocardial uptake with technetium-labeled tracers was first linked to ATTR predominance [15], and pyrophosphate imaging helps distinguish ATTR from AL when interpreted with appropriate technique [16]. A key diagnostic principle is that grade 2–3 cardiac uptake establishes ATTR cardiac amyloidosis without biopsy only when a monoclonal protein screen is negative, because AL can occasionally show uptake [17]. Serum and urine immunofixation plus serum free light-chain assay are therefore mandatory in all suspected cases. When monoclonal gammopathy is present, or imaging is discordant, tissue confirmation and amyloid typing are required; laser microdissection with mass spectrometry is a reference method for accurate amyloid classification [18].

Risk stratification combines symptoms, biomarkers, renal function, rhythm status, and imaging phenotype. Consensus criteria standardized organ involvement and response assessment in AL amyloidosis [19]. Troponin and natriuretic peptide staging established the central prognostic role of cardiac injury and wall stress in AL [20], later refined by adding the involved–uninvolved free light-chain difference [21]. Treatment response in AL is judged by rapid hematologic suppression of amyloidogenic light chains and by cardiac biomarker response, particularly NT-proBNP [22]. ATTR staging systems using NT-proBNP with estimated glomerular filtration rate, or troponin with NT-proBNP, provide practical prognostic classification in both hereditary and wild-type disease [23,24].

Management requires both heart-failure care and disease-modifying therapy. Conventional neurohormonal blockade is often poorly tolerated because stroke volume is fixed and autonomic dysfunction is common. Loop diuretics, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, salt restriction, rhythm management, anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation, and selected pacing are central. Digoxin and non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers are generally avoided or used cautiously. In ATTR cardiomyopathy, tafamidis reduced mortality and cardiovascular hospitalizations and is the established transthyretin stabilizer for symptomatic disease [25]. In AL amyloidosis, urgent plasma-cell–directed therapy is required; daratumumab plus cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone has improved hematologic and organ responses [26]. Autologous stem-cell transplantation remains appropriate for carefully selected AL patients, but randomized data highlighted the hazards of intensive therapy in unselected populations [27]. Gene-silencing therapies such as patisiran and inotersen reduce transthyretin production in hereditary ATTR polyneuropathy and have supported broader therapeutic development for cardiac disease [28,29]. In vivo CRISPR-Cas9 editing of TTR has shown early proof of substantial transthyretin reduction, illustrating the rapidly evolving therapeutic landscape [30].

Earlier recognition is now the major unmet need. Cardiac amyloidosis should be considered in older patients with HFpEF and increased wall thickness, unexplained low-flow aortic stenosis, discordance between wall thickness and ECG voltage, unexplained neuropathy or autonomic dysfunction, or multisystem features. A structured pathway—monoclonal protein testing, cardiac imaging, scintigraphy when appropriate, and definitive typing—allows timely therapy and avoids misclassification between AL and ATTR, the error with the greatest clinical consequence.
